changes.before: Which change safely prints the long variable long count = 3L?
changes.after: A number's type sets its allowed values. Match that type when printing the number.

before: int represents whole numbers; double represents approximate fractional values. C specifies minimum ranges rather than requiring every machine to use the same int width.
INT_MAX in limits.h is the largest int on this implementation. Never assume an int is always exactly 32 bits.
printf uses a format string. %d expects int; %ld expects long; %f expects double for printf. Mismatched argument types can cause undefined behavior, so match them deliberately.
The small values here fit all conforming int implementations. A long literal can use L, but long also has a finite implementation-dependent range.
Expected output or behavior: 3. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Change both the type and its matching format. Explain why output formatting is a type contract rather than a cosmetic label. You may trace it without a C compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: `int` stores whole numbers. `double` can store fractional numbers, often approximately. The exact range of int can differ between machines.
`INT_MAX`, provided by limits.h, gives the largest int on your system. Do not assume int always uses 32 bits. A bit is a single 0 or 1 used to store data.

A format mark tells printf what kind of value to expect. `%d` expects int, `%ld` expects long, and `%f` expects double. A mismatch can cause undefined behavior: C no longer promises what the program will do.
The value 3 fits every standard int range. `long` is another whole-number type with its own limits. The L in `3L` makes that number a long value.
This prints 3. The `%d` mark matches the int variable.
If you change count to long, change the format to `%ld` too. Both describe the same value type; the format is not just a label on the screen.

before.question: Which change safely prints the long variable long count = 3L?
choices: Keep %d because every integer format is interchangeable.
Use %ld so the format matches long.
before.explanation: The variadic printf contract requires the matching type for each format conversion.

after.question: Which format should print the variable in `long count = 3L;`?
choices: %d, because all whole-number formats are the same.
%s, because the number appears as text.
after.explanation: %ld tells printf to read a long value. %d expects int and %s expects a string.
